newsitem.title: USA: GM move further boosts nickel auto battery.
newsitem.headline: GM move further boosts nickel auto battery.

text.p: GM's decision to install nickel metal hydride batteries in their new EV1 electric vehicle and soon-to-be-launched S10 truck, further boosts NMH in a niche hitherto dominated by the lead-acid rival, officials said.
"No question, it's a step forward," Ed Riddell of the U.S. Advanced Battery Consortium which develops and promotes NMH auto batteries.
So far, only test vehicles have used NMH batteries, Riddell said.
USABC paid a big chunk of the battery's development costs and is testing it on behalf of GM for use towards the end of this year.
The lead-acid lobby responded stoically to GM's move.

"It's a very sensible thing for them to do, but I don't think the market for lead-acid batteries in electric vehicles is in any way different from what it has been," Patrick Moseley, program manager for the Advanced Lead Acid Battery Consortium said.
Lead-acid batteries were cheaper, could be charged more quickly than nickel metal hydride units, and were also recyclable, Moseley added.
"We are working very hard to try and do something about the cost," Riddell countered.
Earlier this month GM indicated it was looking to install nickel metal hydride batteries in some EV1s to double mileage between recharges.
"We have not said when that battery will be in the market, but it will be soon," GM spokesman Dick Thompson said. There is no announcement yet on the strategy of using the new battery.

"It will probably be offered as an uplevel option. If the customer wants the extra range, he pays the extra money for it, but that's not official," Thompson said. "We are finding the lead acid battery satisfactory for most people."
Moseley said the lead-acid battery was still set to win a large share of the cheaper range electric vehicle market.
The range for lead-acid battery-equipped EV1 is 70 to 90 miles, but some users have logged over 100 miles as they learn how to drive the car, Thompson added.
GM has built 400 EV1s, and leased 180 at $35,000 a year each in trial markets in Los Angeles, San Diego, Phoenix and Tuscon since the end of last year.
"We planned on a slow start," Dick Thompson, a GM spokesman said. "The letters that we get are overwhelmingly positive."
Some of the owners in California have started an EV1 club.
"They are all high profile - top cinematographers in Hollywood, business people, physicians and attorneys."

Production of GM's new $33,305 S10 truck has just begun with the first one to be delivered May 20. It will be offered to fleet customers only in minimum batches of 10 trucks with a range of 60 miles between recharging.
Dave Barthmuss of Chevrolet, which is marketing the new truck, said pledges for 1,000 trucks have been received.
S10 trucks have lead-acid batteries. "We are looking at nickel metal hydride technology and hoping that will be available soon," Barthmuss said.
Ford unveiled a lead-acid battery-powered version of its Ranger pick-up truck in January, but hoped to offer a version with a NMH pack in October next year.
Riddell said Toyota Motor Corp and Honda Motors Co Ltd will power their electric vehicles by nickel metal hydride when launched in the U.S. at the end of this year to early 1998.
Nissan Motor Co said it planned to use lithium ion batteries in its commercial EV.
